citations.quote: This article presents a development of a CubeSat mission software running on an STM32-based on-board computer (OBC). This was conducted under the Canadian CubeSat Project, initiated by the Canadian Space Agency in 2018 to support the development of 15 CubeSats across Canada.
The CubeSat will be able to accomplish two scientific missions related to the study of space weather once the satellite is put into orbit from the International Space Station.

This work presents a mission software architecture and tests on real developed CubeSat satellite subsystems, such as the OBC, the payload, the communication board, and the backplane to form the FlatSat. This research has been conducted under the Canadian CubeSat Project funded by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) to develop the first Satellite designed in New Brunswick, Canada.

The main goal is to ensure that the majority of the software developed can be ported to different satellites with minimal changes, simply by configuring parameters according to mission requirements; this is especially important for the upper levels, which must remain unaffected even if some lower-level modules change. It also provides a framework that attempts to make the integration of new technologies easier and to allow comparisons of different elements.

The OBSW data pool can contain all operational variables, such as the system time, sensor data, equipment data, eps data (currents and voltages), position and velocity, attitude and rotation measures, and payloads instrument statuses.

The mode transitions generated by a subsystem control are handled by the control application for that subsystem. If a solar panel voltage fails, the EPS subsystem mode may be changed to the EPS Safe Mode. In the Safe Mode, the EPS, for example, only uses batteries to power all the CubeSat and may turn off all payloads.

The following steps make up the complete OBSW development process: software functional analysis, software requirements formulation, software design, software implementation and coding, and software verification and testing.

During the CubeSat development, a complete definition of all on-board functions must be worked up, with specifics on which functions will be implemented in software and which in hardware. For the OBSW, a so-called Function Tree must be built.
The elaboration of precise OBSW requirements follows the definition of the OBSW function tree.

The definition of such requirements is already implemented in database-linked editors in today's systems. Thus, in the same tool environment, a formal linkage of verification activities such as individual test case runs to dedicated requirements and requirement closeout can be recorded.
In any event, OBSW implementation and coding necessitate a significant amount of manual labor.
The development process is a traditional V-model, with design and verification as the primary branches.

The approaches typically follow the guidelines to test from bottom to top, i.e., from hardware interface layers to top-level FDIR, and from inside to outside, such as testing coded controller algorithms in a functional verification bench first, and then the controller embedded in the OBSW framework against a simulated satellite later.
The EPS verifies if the batteries are charged and ensure the satellite is pointing toward the Sun and get the power consumption of all subsystems.
Gitlab is used with the MIT license as a software directory and for version control.

Fig.3 shows the architecture of the CubeSat main bus with its subsystems. The EPS system which comes from ISIS (company specializing in the manufacture of CubeSat) [34] consists of batteries, solar panels, power management and distribution unit is connected to the OBC via I2C communication bus and helps supply energy to the CubeSat other subsystems.

The main goals of the software architecture are reliability, availability, reusability, and scalability. The software is organized in several parts and several layers in order to ensure the operation of the satellite, carry out the missions, manage the mission, accomplish the planned tasks, ensure the communication between the various subsystems and the communication with the ground station, and manage energy consumption, failure, etc. [13], [36]

The breakdown of the system is based on tasks and requirements. The decomposition can be done using the top-down approach where one starts with the general problem and then breaks it down into manageable chunks, one can get a suitable design.

FreeRTOS which is an operating system for embedded systems but it is only used for task management, semaphores, scheduler, and modular programming. So, we will need this system to implement the OBC software. We then need to define the number of tasks and their respective priority levels when running the software.

It was decided to implement the CSP which is a network communication layer in the satellite software. It thus simplifies the communication link and facilitates further development for the other CubeSats projects of the institutions participating in the developments [38], [39].
Some subsystems are purchased with their basic software and therefore cannot use CSP, for example, EPS. We need to write the communication system between these devices separately.
To execute the flight plan contained in the table, we need three tasks, and three queues as shown in Fig. 7.
The Flight plan task retrieves the result of the execution of the command and compared to the result, takes a decision of the next command to perform as shown in arrow 6.

Operating the On-Board Computer: Once the CubeSat is on, the OBC requests the status of all the subsystems, once received we check the voltage of the solar panels if it is not in the desired ranges, we isolate some panels, if the value obtained is correct, we check the battery voltage if incorrect we isolate the defective batteries. Then, we check if the batteries are charged; otherwise, the batteries will be charged; if after 12 h the batteries are not charged, we go into the failure mode to solve the problem.

Currently, the processor load is 34% in normal modes, manual, calibration, and maintenance, and 16% in the failure mode. Of the 1024 kB of flash memory, only 240 kB was used which represents less than 20% of the total memory.

Calibration and Maintenance Mode: This mode should provide the required calibration and maintenance for the mission subsystems. The satellite should enter this mode, based on the status of the subsystems. This may include battery charging, payload calibration, and ADCS.

Our software is designed to run with different hardware, a redefined version of the software will be installed on the other subsystem in order to react to the OBC command accordingly.

Implemented CSP consists of providing the CAN drivers of the microcontroller and integrated into the CSP so that the latter can use it in communication. An example implementation has been provided by CSP for Linux to serve as a guide for integrating CAN but using it as a reference to other systems remains particularly difficult especially on-board systems.
For the CLI we had, it connected to the USB serial adapter over UART. A baud rate of 115200 bits/s with a word length of 8 bits was used for the configuration.

To make sure that the CSP implementation is working properly, it should be tested. Although the best way to test the implementation is on the prototype of the satellite itself, a team of students had already developed what is called FlatSat (a test board with 6 PC104 slots) to connect the satellite modules together in this case the OBC, the communication board, and the OEM7 carrier board for the sending and receiving packets. This means that we can test the modules together and make sure it works before putting it in a real satellite to avoid damage.

The satellite will most likely consist of six modules which must be connected via a CAN link, the OBC, the communication board, the OEM7's carrier board, a camera board, the power supply system, and the control system. Therefore, the tests should prove that the connection will work with more than three modules, and it should be displayed that each module can control the network without reconfiguration.

The tests performed are simple tests that ensure that basic transmissions are transferred successfully over the CAN link and received by a socket listener on the other side of the connection. A beacon message was sent from the OBC to the communication board and successfully received by the ground station. The OBC can communicate with the OEM7 and gather position data from it. Additional testing should be performed when all modules implement CSP to ensure its reliability.

The essential parts of the mission software are presented. The objectives and requirements were defined, the components were also chosen accordingly, then the drivers for these components were written for the mission software.

Software development is a task that is divided into several stages as presented in this document. CSP has been implemented and tested for its basic functionality, the microcontroller CAN driver was developed to communicate with other subsystems since the CSP has no information of the driver used. Positive results are obtained when testing the system, thereby strengthening the development process.

A control system has been implemented to test the OBSW by sending commands to the subsystems through the CSP. A solid configuration of the CSP has been developed with controls which thus provides easier use of the CSP for future software development. It is now possible for students to start integrating CSP with other subsystems with an Implemented Test Tool (CLI).

The application code that will be running on top of the FreeRTOS is also developed for the basic functions such as scheduling, communicating with another subsystem, and confirm messages received with or without packet loss. This application runs using low CPU loads and low memory.
